Father Christmas, five hundred gallons

A Wrexham landlady christened a cask Father Christmas and tapped it on Christmas Eve. Christmas ale was never a style. It was a date, a strength and a piece of theatre.

On Christmas Eve 1858, in Wrexham, a cask of beer was given a name.

Mrs Rowland of the Nag’s Head had been advertising for a fortnight. Her Christmas ale would please the palate and please the eye by its sparkling brilliancy, and would warm and invigorate the whole system. And then the detail that makes it a story rather than a notice: the large cask containing two hundred gallons, and christened Father Christmas, would be tapped on Christmas Eve.

The advert ran under a verse.

Hail! Father Christmas, Hail! to thee, / Honoured ever shalt thou be; / All the sweets that love bestows, / Endless pleasures wait on those / Who, like the vassals brave and true, / Give to Christmas homage due.Wrexham and Denbighshire Advertiser, 24 December 1858

The following Christmas Eve, Father Christmas held five hundred gallons. The lovers of the pure extract of malt and hops were respectfully invited to come and taste it, and the Nag’s Head was illuminated that evening from six till eleven.

Not a style, a date

It is tempting to read all this as evidence of a Victorian beer style, and it is not.

The strongest thing in the record is an absence. Twelve British brewing manuals of the period were searched for the words Christmas, Xmas and Yule: Black, Wigney, Chadwick, Hitchcock, Tizard, Pitt, Southby, Accum, Child, Roberts, Byrn and The Brewer of 1874. Christmas ale is in none of them. The only hits are men keeping Christmas somewhere, which is not a beer.

Everything the Wrexham adverts boast about is in those manuals under other names. Strength is there as stock ale and strong ale. Long ageing is there. October brewing is there, because October was when you brewed what you meant to keep. What is not there is a product called Christmas ale, because Christmas ale was not a thing you brewed. It was a thing you sold.

Which is exactly what the adverts are doing. They sell the tapping, not the recipe. Tapped this day. Tapped on Christmas Eve. Orders should be given immediately. Delivered a fortnight before Christmas Day. In 1869 the Nag’s Head finally says the quiet part out loud and advertises beer brewed in October and matured on the stillage, which is the whole of the method, stated as a selling point rather than a style.

What it cost, and how strong

The price evidence is thin and consistent, which is the best combination available.

The late Martyn Cornell’s reading of Victorian beer adverts puts Christmas ale in the top price tier, alongside No 1 Burton and imperial stout, at two shillings a gallon and an original gravity above 1100. He is careful that not every brewer sold every beer at every price point, and the Wrexham adverts never quote a gravity or a price at all, so the Nag’s Head ale cannot be put on that scale.

Where a number does survive, it is large. Ron Pattinson owns a brewing log from Lovibond, a small London brewer, containing an XXXX ale whose record states it was for Christmas. It was brewed on 7 October 1864, seven weeks ahead, at an original gravity of 1096. Cornell found a Watford brewer selling an XXXXX Christmas Ale at two shillings a gallon in the 1890s, and reasoned from the price that it must have been over 1100.

And in December 1853 a firm in Pall Mall advertised Allsopp’s Strong Christmas Ale as a curiosity for Christmas consumption, the beer originally brewed for the Czar Peter and the Empress Catherine, barrels of which had gone with the expedition sent to look for Sir John Franklin in the Arctic. That beer is Allsopp’s Arctic Ale, which we have written about, and which has spent the last few years being revived on a provenance nobody can quite produce.

The phrase is older than the product

William Sandys, writing on Christmastide, has it that Christmas broached the mightiest ale and that Christmas ale “has, accordingly, been famous from the earliest times”. Welsh papers use the phrase in verse and folklore in 1838, 1839 and 1852, before any of the adverts here.

So the Victorian brewers were not naming something new. They were taking a phrase every reader already knew from carols and country custom, and putting it on a cask.

A warning for anyone counting: Welsh newspaper OCR reads CHRISTMAS SALE as CHRISTMAS ALE, and the Wrexham cattle market ran a Christmas sale of fat stock for years. Any keyword count of the phrase is contaminated by livestock.

The row about the workhouse

The best of it is not in the adverts at all.

On 19 December 1861 the Wrexham Board of Guardians read out letters offering Christmas beer for the workhouse. A publican at the Golden Lion Vaults offered a kilderkin of the best XX stout. A brewer at Wrexham Fechan offered a half barrel of the best beer. So did the Carnarvon Castle Inn. And so did Thomas Rowland of the Nag’s Head, who had worked out why the offers had dried up.

He had heard, he wrote, that no Wrexham brewer intended to send the usual half barrel for the poor on Christmas Day, because of the opposition to be expected from his very enthusiastic teetotal friend, Mr Lester, who would substitute plum cake and coffee instead of beer. Rowland noted that Scripture says wine maketh glad the heart of man, observed that he had no wine, and offered a half barrel of ale, out of his turn, to make glad if possible the hearts of the poor people.

There were a hundred and seventy people in the house.

That argument did not go away. It is still running in Cardiff in 1900 and 1910, where the Guardians voted for beer by twenty-six to twenty-two, and in Colchester in 1922, where a pint a head was carried by twelve votes to five. For the better part of a century, whether the poor got a Christmas drink was decided by a show of hands.

Where it went

The phrase does not fade in the nineteenth century. In 1898 a South Wales columnist is still saying that the good old custom of drinking Christmas ale has not faded in any way by the march of the years, and then grumbling about beer and recommending light wines, which is its own kind of evidence.

What changes is the container. The Brewery History Society puts the earliest known festive bottled beer in the 1930s, either a Christmas Ale from John Fox of Ewloe or one from Simonds, and cannot say which came first because neither is dated. Before that, as the Society puts it, generic strong ales not specifically associated with Christmas had been an integral part of winter for years.

Which is the whole history in one sentence. The beer came first and the label came later.

Will Hawkes gives Harvey’s Christmas Ale, first brewed in 1972 by their head brewer Anthony Jenner, as one of the oldest British Christmas ales still in production, if not the oldest. The wider revival waits for the small breweries of the 1980s. And the beer most people in England now think of as the Christmas one is not called Christmas anything: it is Young’s Winter Warmer, a surviving Burton ale, now brewed by Carlsberg Britvic at the Albion Brewery in Burton on Trent, on a site dating from 1834, which is due to close next summer with the loss of up to three hundred jobs. The cask brands may be contracted out. Nobody will say yet.

In Wrexham the brewery behind the Nag’s Head went in 1984, when Marston’s took over Border Breweries and closed the site. The pub is still there on Mount Street, and Marston’s still run it, and it still does a Christmas menu.

Nobody has christened the cask since.

Winter is not Christmas
A winter beer and a Christmas beer are different things, and Winter Warmer is a name rather than a temperature.
